Estimates of neonatal mass in Tyrannosaurus rex remain highly tentative, given the extreme rarity of very young individuals in the fossil record. Based on the dimensions of the smallest known specimens and extrapolation from egg size in related theropods, a hatchling emerging from the nest likely weighed approximately 3000 grams [Wwb = approximately 3000 grams]. This initial mass indicates a substantial investment per offspring, especially when considered alongside a neonate mass per unit of oxygen consumed of 10 grams per mole , a value that may reflect the metabolic scope required for rapid early growth. The long incubation period and the altricial to precocial transition typical of large theropods would have necessitated considerable parental effort during the first weeks post-hatching. Comparative data from extant archosaurs suggest that such a large hatchling mass is consistent with a relatively small clutch size, as energetic constraints would have limited the number of eggs a gravid female could produce and effectively guard. The few articulated juvenile specimens known hint at a growth trajectory that began steeply, doubling body mass within the first few months of life under optimal conditions, before slowing as skeletal maturity approached in later years.

Recent biomechanical and histological studies have refined our understanding of the ultimate size attained by adult Tyrannosaurus rex. The largest, fully mature individuals are estimated to have reached an ultimate wet weight of approximately 8,000,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 8,000,000 grams], a value derived from femoral circumference and total body length reconstructions. This represents a staggering 2,600-fold increase from the hatchling mass of about 3000 grams [Wwb = about 3000 grams], implying a sustained growth rate that is among the highest ever recorded for a terrestrial vertebrate. Such rapid somatic expansion would have required an enormous daily caloric intake, likely focused on large-bodied herbivorous dinosaurs. The attainment of this massive adult size also has profound implications for the species' metabolic physiology and life history. Comparative analyses with modern crocodilians and birds suggest that the energetic costs of tissue maintenance at this size would have been substantial, and that the growth trajectory likely involved a prolonged juvenile to sub-adult phase before the exponential curve began to plateau as the animal approached its asymptotic dimensions in late adolescence.

The maximum lifespan of Tyrannosaurus rex has been a subject of considerable debate, but growth ring analysis of femoral and tibial bone histology provides the most reliable estimates. Assuming a resting metabolic rate consistent with an endothermic or mesothermic physiology operating at a core body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], skeletal maturity and the completion of the most rapid growth phase appear to have occurred around the end of the second decade. Under these thermal conditions, the oldest documented individuals, based on counts of lines of arrested growth, suggest a maximum longevity of approximately 23,725 days [am = approximately 23,725 days]—equivalent to at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]about 65 years. This is somewhat longer than earlier estimates of around 28 years, but the newer data incorporate a wider sample of senescent adults exhibiting reduced vascularity in the outer cortex. Such a lifespan is remarkable for a large predator and likely reflects a combination of low extrinsic mortality rates in adults, a slow baseline metabolic rate compared to mammals of similar size, and a protracted period of reproductive activity once skeletal growth ceased.

The onset of sexual maturity in Tyrannosaurus rex occurred well before the attainment of maximum adult size, a pattern common among large, long-lived vertebrates. Histological markers such as the transition from fast-growing fibrolamellar bone to slower, more organized lamellar bone indicate that sexual maturation and the attainment of puberty occurred at approximately 18 years since birth [tp = approximately 18 years since birth] at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. At this point, an individual would have already achieved roughly 60 to 70 percent of its ultimate body mass, weighing several tonnes. Importantly, this timing of puberty at 18 years since birth [tp = 18 years since birth] corresponds to a maintenance temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], which is consistent with the thermal regime inferred for active adults from oxygen isotope thermometry. Reaching reproductive maturity at this age would have allowed Tyrannosaurus to begin breeding while still enjoying a high growth potential, likely leading to a period of life in which both somatic and reproductive investment occurred simultaneously. This growth-reproduction overlap is rarely seen in endotherms but is more common in large ectotherms and likely characterized the life history of this apex predator.

Reproductive output in Tyrannosaurus rex remains among the most speculative aspects of its life history, but scaling relationships with modern birds and crocodilians provide a useful framework. Under a core body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], the maximum reproductive rate has been estimated at approximately 160 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 160 eggs per year], derived from metabolic scaling models. This annual output implies a clutch size of perhaps 15 to 20 eggs per nesting event [N_R_i = 15 to 20 eggs per nesting event] and approximately eight to eleven nesting events per year [F_R_i = approximately eight to eleven nesting events per year]. The substantial risk of nest predation by contemporaneous smaller theropods and the demand for intensive parental care likely favored quality over quantity in offspring production. It is also plausible that not every sexually mature female bred each year; environmental fluctuations in prey abundance or individual body condition could have suppressed reproduction in unfavorable seasons. The long lifespan of about 23,725 days [am = about 23,725 days] for individuals maintained at 37 °C would have compensated for a low annual fecundity by providing many potential breeding seasons over a li at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]fetime.
